answer.rationale: Objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, so the response to a competitor price cut should defend value delivery rather than match price. Only two memories have recovered source records this cycle. exp_86 (shortened onboarding) is the strongest: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3% — the only direction with a documented positive retention effect, which is exactly the failure mode a price war creates. Faster time-to-value is also a credible counter to price-driven churn conversations, since accounts that reach first value are less likely to defect on price alone. Promotional pricing is explicitly ruled out as a general strategy by memory_73: it buys acquisition and short-run revenue while materially reducing 30-day retention, and matching a second, deeper cut invites a margin spiral that erodes exactly the metric we are optimizing. Note a memory-drift risk I am acting on cautiously: memory_31 summarizes signup simplification as a 'durable lift' but the recovered source exp_31 shows retention -1%, qualified revenue only +4%, SMB-only, not replicated elsewhere. The consolidated summary is more favorable than its source, so I am weighting exp_86 (shortened onboarding) rather than field-cutting at signup, and I flag memory_31 for correction. memory_57, memory_91, memory_44, and memory_73 have no recovered sources this cycle and may carry similar optimistic drift; referral incentives on established customers are the best second option but do not address the SMB price-sensitive cohort under pressure, and enterprise sales-assist is off-segment for this threat. Scale: standard_experiment, not broad rollout — the +3% retention result predates the current competitive environment and was not measured under active price pressure, so the effect size should be re-estimated with a holdout before company-wide commitment. Guardrails: monitor 30-day retention and qualified revenue in the price-sensitive SMB cohort specifically, and treat any retention regression as a stop condition. If the experiment underperforms, the fallback is referral incentives, not price matching.
